narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 95% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, this was treated as a very high academic-risk signal, not a certainty about your ability, and admission was denied on that basis.

The strongest factor in this prediction was your LSAT score, which at 18 is far below the average of about 37 among accepted students and pushed the prediction toward failure. The next most influential factor was your third-year class-rank decile: you are in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, and this also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class-rank decile, also the lowest and well below the accepted average near the sixth decile, was the third most important factor and added further risk. All three top factors therefore pointed in the same direction: a higher chance of failing the bar.

To improve a future application, focus first on raising your LSAT score through structured preparation and possibly a retake. Meet with academic advisors to address the low class-rank pattern and build a plan for stronger law-school performance. Ask admissions for feedback, document your improvements, and consider reapplying only after showing clear progress. This prediction is a risk estimate, not a final judgment of your potential.
